title: Sintaxis avanzada y estructuras complejas / Advanced syntax and sentence structures
bridge: In English, subordinate clauses are typically introduced by conjunctions like 'that', 'which', or 'if', and word order remains relatively fixed. Spanish offers a more flexible word order, often placing the verb before the subject for emphasis or stylistic effect. Additionally, Spanish uses the subjunctive mood in subordinate clauses to express doubt, emotion, or hypothetical situations—a structure that has no direct equivalent in English. English speakers must learn to recognize when the subjunctive is triggered and to adjust word order to maintain clarity and naturalness.
rule: At C1 level, Spanish syntax allows for a variety of word orders to emphasize different elements, such as fronting objects or adverbials (e.g., 'Eso no lo sé' instead of 'No sé eso'). Subordinate clauses often require the subjunctive when introduced by expressions like 'aunque', 'cuando', 'para que', or 'sin que', depending on the context (e.g., 'Busco un libro que sea interesante' – indefinite antecedent). In complex sentences, subordinate clauses can be placed before or after the main clause, but the verb in the subordinate remains in the appropriate tense and mood. Relative clauses with prepositions, such as 'el cual' or 'lo cual', are common in formal writing. Additionally, Spanish often uses the impersonal 'se' to avoid stating the agent, which can be translated as passive or impersonal constructions in English. Mastery involves recognizing these patterns and using them to create varied, sophisticated sentences.

concept_examples.text: Aunque llueva, iremos al parque.
concept_examples.translation: Even if it rains, we will go to the park.
concept_examples.phonetic: aunˈke ʝweˈβa iˈɾemos al ˈpaɾke

concept_examples.text: El libro que me recomendaste es fascinante.
concept_examples.translation: The book that you recommended to me is fascinating.
concept_examples.phonetic: el ˈliβɾo ke me rekomenˈdaste es fasθiˈnante

concept_examples.text: No sé si haya llegado el tren.
concept_examples.translation: I don't know if the train has arrived.
concept_examples.phonetic: no ˈse si ˈaʝa ʝeˈɣaðo el tɾen

concept_examples.text: Para que todos entiendan, hay que explicarlo con calma.
concept_examples.translation: So that everyone understands, we must explain it calmly.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈpaɾa ke ˈtoðos entˈjenðan ai ke ekspliˈkaɾlo kon ˈkalma

common_error.wrong: No sé si ha llegado el tren.
common_error.correct: No sé si haya llegado el tren.
common_error.correct_alt: No sé si llegó el tren.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use the indicative 'ha llegado' because they directly translate 'I don't know if it has arrived'. However, after 'no sé si' (I don't know whether), when the outcome is uncertain, Spanish often uses the subjunctive 'haya llegado' to express doubt. The indicative would be used if the truth were known. To avoid this error, memorize that uncertainty or doubt triggered by 'no sé si' typically requires the subjunctive.

examples.original: Cuando vengas, avísame.
examples.phonetic: ˈkwando ˈbeŋɡas aˈβisame
examples.translation: When you come, let me know.
examples.note: Use subjunctive after 'cuando' when referring to future actions.

examples.original: Aunque estudies mucho, podrías fracasar.
examples.phonetic: aunˈke estuˈðjes ˈmutʃo poˈðɾias fɾakaˈsaɾ
examples.translation: Even if you study a lot, you could fail.
examples.note: Subjunctive after 'aunque' when the concession is hypothetical.

examples.original: La persona con quien hablé es doctora.
examples.phonetic: la peɾˈsona kon kjen aˈβle es dokˈtoɾa
examples.translation: The person with whom I spoke is a doctor.
examples.note: Use 'con quien' instead of 'con que' in formal Spanish.

examples.original: El tema del cual me hablaste es complejo.
examples.phonetic: el ˈtema del ˈkwal me aˈβlaste es komˈplexo
examples.translation: The topic about which you spoke to me is complex.
examples.note: Use 'del cual' to express 'which' after a preposition.

examples.original: He visto muchos países, lo cual me ha enriquecido.
examples.phonetic: e ˈβisto ˈmutʃos paˈises lo kwal me a enrikeˈθiðo
examples.translation: I have visited many countries, which has enriched me.
examples.note: 'lo cual' refers to the whole previous clause.

examples.original: Eso nunca lo entenderé.
examples.phonetic: ˈeso ˈnuŋka lo entendeˈɾe
examples.translation: That I will never understand.
examples.note: Fronting the object 'eso' for emphasis, reserving the pronoun 'lo' to avoid duplication.

examples.original: Difícil es la vida del inmigrante.
examples.phonetic: diˈfil ˈes la ˈβiða del inmiˈɣɾante
examples.translation: Difficult is the life of the immigrant.
examples.note: Adjective fronted for contrastive emphasis.

examples.original: No es fácil entender la poesía de Góngora.
examples.phonetic: no es ˈfaθil entenˈdeɾ la poeˈsia de ˈɣongɡora
examples.translation: It is not easy to understand Góngora's poetry.
examples.note: Impersonal 'it' is omitted in Spanish.

examples.original: Para mí, eso es un problema.
examples.phonetic: ˈpaɾa mi ˈeso es un pɾoˈβlema
examples.translation: For me, that is a problem.
examples.note: Fronting 'para mí' as a topic marker.

title: Registro y estilo: formal, informal y neutro / Register and style: formal, informal and neutral
bridge: In English, register shifts are often achieved through vocabulary choice and contractions (e.g., 'can't' vs 'cannot'), but Spanish has a more systematic approach: the use of 'tú' vs 'usted' (and their verb forms) signals formality, while 'vosotros' vs 'ustedes' distinguishes informal plural in Spain. Additionally, Spanish uses the passive 'se' and impersonal 'uno' to achieve a neutral/formal tone, whereas English might use 'one' or passive voice. The trap: English speakers often overuse 'tú' in formal contexts because they rely on context, but Spanish requires explicit grammatical markers. Also, informal Spanish drops subject pronouns more freely, while formal written Spanish often includes them for clarity.
rule: In Spanish, register is marked by pronoun choice (tú/usted, vosotros/ustedes), verb conjugations, and lexical formality. Formal register: use 'usted' with third-person singular verb forms, often accompanied by 'su' (formal possessive) and 'le/les' (formal object pronouns). In Spain, 'vosotros' (informal plural) vs 'ustedes' (formal plural); in Latin America, 'ustedes' is used for both, but verb forms remain third-person. Neutral/written register: avoids emotional or colloquial expressions, uses impersonal 'se' ('se dice'), 'uno' ('uno piensa'), and subjunctive in subordinate clauses. Informal register: uses 'tú' forms, contractions (pa' instead of para), and colloquial vocabulary. For C1, control of register includes choosing between synonyms like 'hablar' vs 'conversar' (more formal) or 'empezar' vs 'comenzar' (slightly more formal). Passive 'se' is common in formal writing: 'Se ha decidido que...' instead of 'Han decidido que...' (active, informal). Avoid mixing registers: e.g., using 'tú' with formal vocabulary is inconsistent.

concept_examples.text: ¿Podría usted indicarme dónde está la estación?
concept_examples.translation: Could you tell me where the station is?
concept_examples.phonetic: /pwo'ðɾia us'teɾ indikaɾme 'donde es'ta la esta'θjon/

concept_examples.text: Oye, ¿me pasas la sal?
concept_examples.translation: Hey, can you pass me the salt?
concept_examples.phonetic: /'oʝe me 'pasas la sal/

concept_examples.text: Se ha observado un aumento en las ventas.
concept_examples.translation: An increase in sales has been observed.
concept_examples.phonetic: /se a obser'βado un au'mento en las 'bentas/

concept_examples.text: Uno debe ser responsable de sus actos.
concept_examples.translation: One must be responsible for one's actions.
concept_examples.phonetic: /'uno 'deβe ser respon'saβle de sus 'aktos/

common_error.wrong: ¿Puedes decirme dónde está el banco? (said in a formal context to a stranger)
common_error.correct: ¿Podría usted decirme dónde está el banco?
common_error.correct_alt: ¿Me podría indicar dónde está el banco?
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use the informal 'puedes' with a stranger because English does not distinguish verb forms based on politeness to the same extent. In Spanish, using 'tú' with a stranger can sound rude or overly familiar. To avoid this, use 'usted' forms ('podría' instead of 'puedes') and the formal pronoun 'usted' explicitly or implicitly, and consider using conditional ('podría') as a politeness marker.

levels.label: Pronombres de tratamiento: tú vs. usted
levels.translation: Forms of address: tú vs. usted

examples.original: Tú tienes mucha suerte, ¿verdad?
examples.phonetic: /tu 'tjenes 'mutʃa 'sweɾte βeɾ'ðað/
examples.translation: You are very lucky, right?
examples.note: Informal singular, used with friends, family, or peers. Notice the verb form 'tienes' (second person singular).

examples.original: Usted tiene mucha suerte, ¿verdad?
examples.phonetic: /us'teɾ 'tjenes 'mutʃa 'sweɾte βeɾ'ðað/
examples.translation: You are very lucky, right?
examples.note: Formal singular, used with strangers, elders, or in professional settings. Verb form 'tiene' (third person singular).

examples.original: Nosotros, en cambio, no tenemos tanta prisa.
examples.phonetic: /no'sotɾos en 'kambjo no te'nemos 'tanta 'pɾisa/
examples.translation: We, on the other hand, are not in such a hurry.
examples.note: Neutral register; uses 'nosotros' explicitly for emphasis, which is common in written formal discourse.

examples.original: Se prohíbe fumar en este establecimiento.
examples.phonetic: /se pɾo'iβe fu'maɾ en 'este estaβlesi'mjento/
examples.translation: Smoking is prohibited in this establishment.
examples.note: Passive 'se' for formal announcements, equivalent to English passive voice.

examples.original: Se dice que va a llover mañana.
examples.phonetic: /se 'diθe ke ba a ʎo'βeɾ ma'ɲana/
examples.translation: They say it's going to rain tomorrow.
examples.note: Impersonal 'se' with 'decir' to express general belief without specifying an agent.

examples.original: Uno no sabe qué pensar.
examples.phonetic: /'uno no 'saβe ke pen'saɾ/
examples.translation: One doesn't know what to think.
examples.note: 'Uno' as impersonal subject, more formal than 'tú' generic.

levels.label: Léxico y estructuras formales vs. informales
levels.translation: Formal vs. informal vocabulary and structures

examples.original: Estimado señor García: le agradezco su atención a este asunto.
examples.phonetic: /esti'maðo se'ɲoɾ gaɾ'si.a le aɣɾa'ðeθko su aten'θjon a 'este a'sunto/
examples.translation: Dear Mr. García: I thank you for your attention to this matter.
examples.note: Formal written register: 'estimado' for 'dear' and 'agradezco' (I thank) instead of 'gracias'.

examples.original: Oye, ¿te vienes al cine o qué?
examples.phonetic: /'oʝe te 'bjenes al 'θine o 'ke/
examples.translation: Hey, are you coming to the movies or what?
examples.note: Informal register: 'oye' as attention-getter, 'te vienes' (colloquial), and 'o qué' for casual questioning.

examples.original: Asimismo, cabe destacar que los resultados fueron positivos.
examples.phonetic: /asi'mismo 'kaβe desta'kaɾ ke los resul'taðos 'fweɾon posi'tiβos/
examples.translation: Likewise, it should be noted that the results were positive.
examples.note: Formal connectors ('asimismo', 'cabe destacar') used in academic or business writing.

title: Inversión y frontalización avanzadas / Advanced inversion and fronting
bridge: In English, inversion is mostly limited to questions and a few fixed expressions (e.g., 'Never have I seen...'). Spanish, however, uses fronting more freely to shift emphasis without changing the word order to subject-verb inversion in the same way. For example, English requires an auxiliary ('Not only did she sing...'), while Spanish simply moves the object or adverb to the front and may leave the verb in its usual position: 'Solo entonces comprendió' (Only then did he understand). The challenge for English speakers is to resist the impulse to add auxiliary verbs or to over-invert, since Spanish often uses fronting without any change in verb-subject order, or uses the personal 'a' to mark objects.
rule: In Spanish, fronting (moving an element to the beginning of a sentence for emphasis or discourse cohesion) is common at C1 level. Unlike English, it rarely triggers grammatical inversion (verb before subject) except in certain fixed structures. Key patterns include: VOS (verb-object-subject) order for emphasis, fronting of objects with the personal 'a' (A María la vi ayer), fronting of adverbs (Bien está lo que bien acaba), and fronting of the predicate in copular sentences (Muy inteligente es ella). Also important are the structures 'el que/la que' + verb for cleft sentences (Fue Juan el que lo dijo) and the use of 'por poco y + subjunctive' for near-miss events. Negative and restrictive expressions such as 'jamás', 'en mi vida' can trigger inversion with preterite or subjunctive (Jamás había visto tal cosa).

concept_examples.text: Solo entonces comprendió la verdad.
concept_examples.translation: Only then did he understand the truth.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈsolo enˈtonθes kоm.pɾenˈdjo la βeɾˈðað

concept_examples.text: A María la vi ayer en el parque.
concept_examples.translation: María, I saw her yesterday in the park.
concept_examples.phonetic: a maˈɾi.a la βi aˈʝeɾ en el ˈpaɾ.ke

concept_examples.text: Muy inteligente es ella.
concept_examples.translation: Very intelligent is she. (She is very intelligent.)
concept_examples.phonetic: mwi in.te.liˈxen.te ˈes ˈe.ʝa

concept_examples.text: Fue Juan el que lo dijo.
concept_examples.translation: It was Juan who said it.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈfwe ˈxwan el ke lo ˈdi.xo

common_error.wrong: Solo entonces él comprendió la verdad.
common_error.correct: Solo entonces comprendió él la verdad.
common_error.correct_alt: Solo entonces comprendió la verdad él.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, when fronting 'solo entonces' (only then), the subject usually moves after the verb, similar to English inversion, but without an auxiliary. Learners often keep the subject in its usual preverbal position, which sounds unnatural in this emphatic construction. To avoid this, remember that fronted adverbs like 'solo entonces', 'jamás', 'ni siquiera' often trigger verb-subject inversion in formal Spanish. Keep the verb before the subject, and omit any auxiliary.

examples.original: A los estudiantes les importa la nota.
examples.phonetic: a los es.tuˈdjan.tes les imˈpoɾ.ta la ˈno.ta
examples.translation: The grade matters to the students.
examples.note: Fronting the indirect object 'a los estudiantes' emphasizes it; the indirect object pronoun 'les' is repeated.

examples.original: Ese libro lo leí hace años.
examples.phonetic: ˈe.se ˈli.βɾo lo leˈi ˈa.θe ˈa.ɲos
examples.translation: That book, I read it years ago.
examples.note: Fronted direct object is repeated with 'lo' – this is obligatory when the fronted object is definite and not a person.

examples.original: Azúcar no me des, que estoy a dieta.
examples.phonetic: aˈθu.kaɾ no me des ke esˈtoi a ˈdje.ta
examples.translation: Don't give me sugar, because I'm on a diet.
examples.note: Fronted noun 'azúcar' without article, not repeated with pronoun; typical in commands.

levels.label: Adverbios y expresiones negativas al inicio
levels.translation: Adverbs and negative expressions at the beginning

examples.original: Jamás había visto un cielo tan claro.
examples.phonetic: xaˈmas aˈβi.a ˈbis.to un ˈθje.lo tan ˈkla.ɾo
examples.translation: Never had I seen such a clear sky.
examples.note: Negative expression 'jamás' fronted triggers verb-subject inversion, but the subject is often omitted; 'había' is auxiliary.

examples.original: En mi vida he probado un plato tan picante.
examples.phonetic: en mi ˈβi.ða e pɾoˈβa.ðo un ˈpla.to tam piˈkan.te
examples.translation: In my life have I tasted such a spicy dish.
examples.note: Common fixed expression; inversion happens but subject omitted, so verb before auxiliary? Actually 'he probado' is compound.

examples.original: Ni siquiera me miró al entrar.
examples.phonetic: ni siˈkje.ɾa me miˈɾo al enˈtɾaɾ
examples.translation: He didn't even look at me when he came in.
examples.note: Fronted 'ni siquiera' does not require inversion; typical spoken use.

examples.original: No solo perdió el partido, sino que se lesionó.
examples.phonetic: no ˈso.lo peɾˈðjo el paɾˈti.ðo | ˈsi.no ke se le.sjoˈno
examples.translation: Not only did he lose the match, but he also got injured.
examples.note: Fronted 'no solo' is followed by verb, not subject; similar to English auxiliary inversion but without 'did'.

examples.original: Apenas había llegado cuando empezó a llover.
examples.phonetic: aˈpe.nas aˈβi.a ʝeˈɣa.ðo ˈkwan.do em.peˈθo a ʎoˈβeɾ
examples.translation: Hardly had he arrived when it started to rain.
examples.note: Inversion with 'apenas' – verb before subject, but subject usually omitted; optional inversion.

examples.original: Así es como se hace.
examples.phonetic: aˈsi es ˈko.mo se ˈa.θe
examples.translation: This is how it's done.
examples.note: Fronted 'así' with verb 'es' – typical fixed structure.

title: Nominalización compleja / Complex Nominalization
bridge: In English, we often turn verbs into nouns by adding suffixes like '-tion' (process → processing) or '-ment' (develop → development). Spanish does this too, but with different suffixes and often different word order. For instance, 'processing' becomes 'el procesamiento' or 'la procesión' (with a change in meaning), and Spanish often uses an infinitive or a 'que' clause where English might use a gerund. A key trap is that Spanish nouns sometimes change gender and require an article, while English nouns are unmarked. Also, Spanish nominalizations can be more flexible, allowing for both the process (procesamiento) and the result (proceso) as distinct nouns.
rule: In Spanish, complex nominalization refers to the formation of nouns from verbs (or adjectives) to express an action, process, or result. Common suffixes include: -ción/-sión (from -ar verbs: transformar → transformación; from -er/-ir: decidir → decisión), -miento (from -ar: tratar → tratamiento; from -er: conocer → conocimiento), -aje (from -ar: almacenar → almacenaje), -ancia/-encia (from -ar: crear → creación, but also from adjectives: frecuente → frecuencia; from verbs: sufrir → sufrencia, though less common). For C1, focus on nuances: the same verb may have multiple nominalizations (e.g., procesar → 'proceso' (result/process) and 'procesamiento' (act of processing)), and the choice depends on whether you refer to the action in progress or the outcome. Spanish also uses the infinitive as a nominal (el fumar) for habitual or abstract actions, and this is more common than in English. Gender is crucial: most nominalizations ending in -ción/-sión are feminine, while those ending in -miento/-aje are masculine. Articles are required. The suffix -ción/-sión often corresponds to English '-tion/-sion' (transformación → transformation), but beware of false friends: 'realización' can mean 'fulfilment' or 'production', not just 'realization' (awareness). When a verb has an irregular participle, the nominalization may derive from that participle (e.g., hacer → hecho, but 'hechura' is rare; instead 'realización'). Also, some nominalizations are fixed and idiomatic. At C1, you should use nominalizations to replace entire clauses for conciseness and sophistication.

concept_examples.text: El procesamiento de datos requiere atención.
concept_examples.translation: Data processing requires attention.
concept_examples.phonetic: el pɾoθesaˈmjento ðe ˈðatos reˈkjeɾe atenˈθjon

concept_examples.text: La transformación del paisaje fue gradual.
concept_examples.translation: The transformation of the landscape was gradual.
concept_examples.phonetic: la tɾansfoɾmaˈθjon ðel paiˈsaxe fwe ɣɾaˈðwal

concept_examples.text: El conocimiento del idioma abre puertas.
concept_examples.translation: Knowing the language opens doors.
concept_examples.phonetic: el konoθiˈmjento ðel iˈðjoma ˈaβɾe ˈpweɾtas

concept_examples.text: La decisión del jurado fue final.
concept_examples.translation: The jury's decision was final.
concept_examples.phonetic: la ðeθiˈsjon del xuˈɾaðo fwe fiˈnal

common_error.wrong: El procesar de los datos es rápido.
common_error.correct: El procesamiento de los datos es rápido.
common_error.correct_alt: El proceso de los datos es rápido.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use the infinitive 'el procesar' as a nominal, but in Spanish, when a specific suffix is available, it's preferred over the infinitive. 'Procesar' as a nominal would be used only in abstract or habitual contexts, but here the process is specific, so 'procesamiento' (action) or 'proceso' (process/result) is correct. Avoid translating the English gerund directly with an infinitive; use the appropriate nominalization.

examples.original: La creación de empleo es prioridad.
examples.phonetic: la kɾeaˈθjon de emˈpleo es pɾjoɾiˈðað
examples.translation: Job creation is a priority.
examples.note: The suffix -ción is highly productive, equivalent to '-tion' in English. Note the feminine article 'la'.

examples.original: El mantenimiento del equipo es esencial.
examples.phonetic: el mantenimjento del eˈkipo es esenˈθjal
examples.translation: Maintenance of the equipment is essential.
examples.note: -miento is common for -er/-ir verbs, but 'mantenimiento' comes from 'mantener'. It is masculine.

examples.original: El aterrizaje fue suave.
examples.phonetic: el ateɾiˈθaxe fwe ˈswaβe
examples.translation: The landing was smooth.
examples.note: -aje is used for actions (e.g., 'aterrizar' → 'aterrizaje'), often corresponding to English '-ing' or '-age'.

examples.original: La construcción del puente duró años.
examples.phonetic: la konstɾukˈθjon del ˈpwente duˈɾo ˈaɲos
examples.translation: The construction of the bridge lasted years.
examples.note: Here 'construcción' refers to the action/process. The result is 'el puente' itself, not a nominal.

examples.original: El crecimiento económico es lento.
examples.phonetic: el kɾeθiˈmjento ekonoˈmiko es ˈlento
examples.translation: Economic growth is slow.
examples.note: 'Crecimiento' is the process; the result is 'el crecimiento' as a state. English uses 'growth' for both, but Spanish may use 'crecimiento' for both as well, but context matters.

examples.original: La administración del sistema es compleja.
examples.phonetic: la administɾaˈθjon del sisˈtema es komˈplexa
examples.translation: The administration of the system is complex.
examples.note: Compare 'administración' (action) with 'administración' (body of officials). The same word can serve both, but the article and context clarify.

examples.original: El desarrollo de nuevas tecnologías avanza.
examples.phonetic: el desaˈʎoʎo de ˈnewas teknoˈloxias aˈβanθa
examples.translation: The development of new technologies advances.
examples.note: Note 'desarrollo' from 'desarrollar' - here it's the process. Different from 'desarrollo' as result (e.g., 'un desarrollo' meaning a development).

levels.label: Nominalización con infinitivo y sustantivos derivados
levels.translation: Nominalization with infinitive and derived nouns

examples.original: El fumar es perjudicial para la salud.
examples.phonetic: el fuˈmaɾ es peɾxuðiˈθjal paɾa la saˈluð
examples.translation: Smoking is harmful to health.
examples.note: The infinitive 'fumar' as a nominal is used for habitual actions. English uses a gerund. This is acceptable when no specific suffix is common.

examples.original: El saber no ocupa lugar.
examples.phonetic: el saˈβeɾ no oˈkupa luˈɣaɾ
examples.translation: Knowledge doesn't take up space.
examples.note: 'Saber' as a noun means 'knowledge', but it's an infinitive. Avoid overusing; when a standard noun exists, use it.

examples.original: La realización del proyecto fue un éxito.
examples.phonetic: la realiθaˈθjon del pɾoˈxeto fwe un ˈeksito
examples.translation: The completion of the project was a success.
examples.note: Remember 'realización' often means 'carrying out', not 'realization' (awakening). This is a classic false friend; use 'realización' for 'achievement/completion', and 'darse cuenta' for 'realize'.

examples.original: El aprendizaje es continuo.
examples.phonetic: el apɾendiˈsaxe es konˈtinwo
examples.translation: Learning is continuous.
examples.note: From 'aprender', the nominal 'aprendizaje' (masculine) is common. English uses 'learning' as a gerund, but Spanish takes a suffix.

title: Elipsis y sustitución: so do I, neither have we / Ellipsis and substitution
bridge: In English, you use auxiliary verbs (do, have, will) to avoid repetition: 'I love it' → 'So do I'. Spanish generally does not use a single auxiliary verb in the same way; instead, it repeats the main verb, uses 'también'/'tampoco', or employs pronominal forms like 'lo' or 'ello'. The biggest trap is overusing 'también' with the wrong verb form, or trying to use 'do' as an auxiliary in Spanish (which doesn't exist except in questions/negatives).
rule: In Spanish, ellipsis (omitting words) and substitution (replacing with pronouns or adverbs) are common to avoid repetition. For agreement with a statement, you use 'también' (also) with the same verb or 'yo también' / 'a mí también' for emphasis. For disagreement, use 'yo no' or 'a mí no'. For negative agreement, use 'tampoco' (neither). For substitution of a previously mentioned verb phrase, Spanish frequently uses 'lo' (it/that) or 'hacerlo' (do it). At C1, you must master the subtle distinctions between 'yo también', 'a mí también', 'también lo hago', and when to use 'también' vs 'tampoco' with different verb tenses. Unlike English, there is no inversion with auxiliary verbs; the structure is simply 'sujeto + también/tampoco + verbo'.

concept_examples.text: —Me encanta el café. —A mí también.
concept_examples.translation: —I love coffee. —Me too.
concept_examples.phonetic: me ɛnˈkanta el kaˈfe | a mi ˈtambjen

concept_examples.text: —No he terminado el informe. —Yo tampoco.
concept_examples.translation: —I haven't finished the report. —Neither have I.
concept_examples.phonetic: no e tɛrmiˈnado el inˈfɔrme | ʝo tamˈpoko

concept_examples.text: —¿Puedes ayudarme? —Sí, claro, lo haré.
concept_examples.translation: —Can you help me? —Yes, of course, I'll do it.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈpweðes aʝuˈðaɾme | si ˈklaɾo lo aˈɾe

concept_examples.text: —Estudias mucho. —Sí, lo hago todas las noches.
concept_examples.translation: —You study a lot. —Yes, I do it every night.
concept_examples.phonetic: esˈtuðjas ˈmutʃo | si lo ˈaɣo ˈtoðas las ˈnotʃes

common_error.wrong: —Me gusta el vino. —Sí, también me gusta. (instead of a short reply)
common_error.correct_alt: —Me gusta el vino. —A mí me gusta también.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often transfer the English pattern 'I like it too' by repeating the full verb phrase. In Spanish, when the verb is the same, you use 'a mí también' or 'yo también' (with the verb implicit). Saying 'también me gusta' is grammatical but redundant and unnatural in a short reply. Avoid translating 'do' as an auxiliary; instead, use 'lo' to substitute the action.

examples.original: —Voy al cine. —Yo también.
examples.phonetic: boi al ˈsine | ʝo ˈtambjen
examples.translation: —I'm going to the movies. —Me too.
examples.note: Use 'yo también' when the subject is the same person (I).

examples.original: —No como carne. —Yo tampoco.
examples.phonetic: no ˈkomo ˈkaɾne | ʝo tamˈpoko
examples.translation: —I don't eat meat. —Neither do I.
examples.note: For negative agreement, use 'tampoco' (neither).

examples.original: —Estoy cansado. —Yo no.
examples.phonetic: esˈtoi kanˈsado | ʝo no
examples.translation: —I'm tired. —I'm not.
examples.note: For disagreement, simply use 'yo no' without repeating the verb.

examples.original: —¿Puedes traer el libro? —Sí, lo traeré.
examples.phonetic: ˈpweðes tɾaˈeɾ el ˈliβɾo | si lo tɾaeˈɾe
examples.translation: —Can you bring the book? —Yes, I'll bring it.
examples.note: 'lo' replaces the direct object (the book).

examples.original: —Estudias francés. —Sí, lo estudio desde hace años.
examples.phonetic: esˈtuðjas fɾanˈθes | si lo esˈtuðjo ˈðesðe ˈaθe ˈaɲos
examples.translation: —You study French. —Yes, I've been studying it for years.
examples.note: 'lo' replaces the entire noun phrase 'francés'.

examples.original: —¿Vas a limpiar? —Sí, lo haré mañana.
examples.phonetic: bas a limˈpjaɾ | si lo aˈɾe maˈɲana
examples.translation: —Are you going to clean? —Yes, I'll do it tomorrow.
examples.note: 'hacerlo' substitutes a previously mentioned action, similar to 'do it'.

levels.label: Elipsis avanzada con verbos modales y tiempos compuestos
levels.translation: Advanced ellipsis with modal verbs and compound tenses

examples.original: —Debes estudiar más. —Ya lo sé, pero no tengo tiempo.
examples.phonetic: ˈdeβes estuˈðjaɾ mas | ʝa lo se ˈpeɾo no ˈteŋɡo ˈtjempo
examples.translation: —You should study more. —I know, but I don't have time.
examples.note: 'lo sé' (I know it) is a fixed expression using 'lo' to refer to the idea.

examples.original: —Habría viajado si hubiera podido, pero no pude.
examples.phonetic: aˈβɾia βjaˈxaðo si uˈβjeɾa poˈðiðo ˈpeɾo no ˈpuðe
examples.translation: —I would have traveled if I had been able, but I couldn't.
examples.note: Here 'no pude' omits the infinitive 'viajar' because it's understood from context.

examples.original: —¿Te gustaría venir? —Sí, me encantaría.
examples.phonetic: te ɣustaˈɾia beˈniɾ | si me enkantaˈɾia
examples.translation: —Would you like to come? —Yes, I'd love to.
examples.note: The verb 'venir' is omitted after 'me encantaría' – a common ellipsis in responses.

title: Marcadores discursivos avanzados para cohesión / Advanced Discourse Markers for Cohesion
bridge: English uses discourse markers like 'however', 'therefore', and 'in addition' to structure arguments, but Spanish has a richer set that often carry more specific nuances. For example, 'sin embargo' (however) is more formal than 'pero', and 'no obstante' adds a subtle concession that 'but' misses. English speakers often overuse 'pero' and 'y' in Spanish, missing the nuance of markers like 'ahora bien' (that said) or 'por consiguiente' (consequently). Watch out for false friends: 'actualmente' means 'currently', not 'actually', and 'eventualmente' means 'possibly', not 'eventually'.
rule: Discourse markers (marcadores discursivos) are words or phrases that connect ideas and guide the listener through the structure of the discourse. At C1, you should move beyond basic connectors and use a variety that convey logical relationships, contrast, concession, cause-effect, reformulation, and exemplification. Key categories include: 1) Addition: 'además', 'asímismo', 'encima' (colloquial). 2) Contrast/Concession: 'sin embargo', 'no obstante', 'ahora bien', 'eso sí', 'en cambio'. 3) Cause/Effect: 'por lo tanto', 'por consiguiente', 'en consecuencia'. 4) Reformulation: 'es decir', 'o sea', 'en otras palabras'. 5) Exemplification: 'por ejemplo', 'así', 'tal como'. 6) Ordering: 'en primer lugar', 'luego', 'finalmente'. Note that many markers have a fixed position in the sentence: they are often set off by commas. Some, like 'sin embargo', can appear at the start, middle, or end, but their placement changes emphasis. In formal writing, avoid using 'encima' or 'o sea' – they are too colloquial. Also, be careful when contrasting with 'pero': it is restrictive, whereas 'sino' is used after a negative to introduce a correction (e.g., 'no solo X, sino Y'). At C1, you should vary your markers to avoid repetition and to signal specific rhetorical effects.

concept_examples.text: La economía crece, sin embargo, hay sectores que siguen en crisis.
concept_examples.translation: The economy is growing; however, there are sectors still in crisis.
concept_examples.phonetic: /la e.ko.noˈmi.a ˈkɾe.se ˈsin emˈbaɾ.ɣo aj sekˈto.ɾes ke ˈsi.ɣen en ˈkɾi.sjas/

concept_examples.text: No estoy de acuerdo con su propuesta; por consiguiente, no la apoyaré.
concept_examples.translation: I don't agree with his proposal; consequently, I will not support it.
concept_examples.phonetic: /no esˈtoj de aˈkweɾ.ðo kon su pɾoˈpwes.ta poɾ kon.siˈɣjen.te no la a.po.ʝaˈɾe/

concept_examples.text: Ahora bien, los resultados no fueron del todo positivos.
concept_examples.translation: That said, the results were not entirely positive.
concept_examples.phonetic: /aˈo.ɾa βjen los re.sulˈta.ðos no ˈfwe.ɾon del ˈto.ðo po.siˈti.βos/

concept_examples.text: El proyecto es ambicioso, en otras palabras, un gran desafío.
concept_examples.translation: The project is ambitious; in other words, a great challenge.
concept_examples.phonetic: /el pɾoˈʝek.to es am.biˈsjo.so en ˈo.tɾas paˈla.βɾas un gɾan de.saˈfi.o/

common_error.wrong: No estuvo de acuerdo con la propuesta, pero apoyó la decisión.
common_error.correct: No estuvo de acuerdo con la propuesta; sin embargo, apoyó la decisión.
common_error.correct_alt: No estuvo de acuerdo con la propuesta; no obstante, apoyó la decisión.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use 'pero' (but) to connect two contrasting ideas, but in more formal or nuanced writing, 'pero' sounds too weak and informal when you want to express a concession. 'Sin embargo' or 'no obstante' are better for contrast in formal contexts, and they require a comma or a semicolon before them. Additionally, 'pero' cannot be used after a negative clause to introduce a positive alternative (that requires 'sino').

examples.original: Además de ser inteligente, es muy trabajadora.
examples.phonetic: /aˈðe.mas de seɾ in.te.liˈxen.te es ˈmwi tɾa.βaˈxo.ɾa/
examples.translation: In addition to being intelligent, she is very hardworking.
examples.note: 'Además' is used to add an idea, but note that it can appear at the beginning or in the middle, and it's often followed by 'de' + infinitive or noun.

examples.original: No me gusta el fútbol, en cambio me encanta el baloncesto.
examples.phonetic: /no me ˈɣus.ta el ˈfut.βol en ˈkam.bo me enˈkan.ta el βa.lonˈθes.to/
examples.translation: I don't like soccer; in contrast, I love basketball.
examples.note: 'En cambio' is used for a contrasting idea between two elements, similar to 'on the other hand', but it can also imply a compensation or replacement.

examples.original: Probé la sopa, pero estaba demasiado salada.
examples.phonetic: /pɾoˈβe la ˈso.pa pe.ɾo esˈta.βa de.maˈsja.ðo saˈla.ða/
examples.translation: I tried the soup, but it was too salty.
examples.note: Here 'pero' is correct because it's a simple contrast between two clauses. Learn to distinguish when 'pero' is enough and when you need a more formal marker like 'sin embargo'.

examples.original: Llueve mucho, por lo tanto el partido se ha suspendido.
examples.phonetic: /ˈʎwe.βe ˈmu.tʃo poɾ lo ˈtan.to el paɾˈti.ðo se a sus.penˈdi.ðo/
examples.translation: It rains a lot, therefore the match has been suspended.
examples.note: 'Por lo tanto' is the most neutral way to express consequence; it is common in both spoken and written Spanish.

examples.original: El equipo no entrenó lo suficiente; en consecuencia, perdió el campeonato.
examples.phonetic: /el eˈki.po no enˈtɾe.no lo su.fiˈθjen.te en kon.seˈɣwjen.sa peɾˈðjo el kam.pe.oˈna.to/
examples.translation: The team didn't train enough; consequently, they lost the championship.
examples.note: 'En consecuencia' is more formal than 'por lo tanto' and is often used in academic or professional writing.

examples.original: No estudiaste, así que no puedes quejarte.
examples.phonetic: /no es.tuˈðjas.te a.si ke no ˈpwe.ðes keˈxaɾ.te/
examples.translation: You didn't study, so you can't complain.
examples.note: 'Así que' is more colloquial and conversational, equivalent to 'so' in English. Use it in informal contexts.

examples.original: La situación es compleja; es decir, no es tan sencilla como parece.
examples.phonetic: /la si.twaˈθjon es komˈple.xa es deˈsiɾ no es tan senˈθi.ʎa ko.mo paˈɾe.θe/
examples.translation: The situation is complex; that is, it is not as simple as it seems.
examples.note: 'Es decir' is the most common reformulator, equivalent to 'that is' or 'i.e.' in English. It is used to clarify or explain something in other words.

examples.original: Algunos países, por ejemplo, España y México, tienen dialectos muy ricos.
examples.phonetic: /alˈɣu.nos paˈi.ses poɾ eˈxem.plo esˈpa.ɲa i ˈme.xi.ko ˈtje.nen dj.aˈlek.tos mwi ˈri.kos/
examples.translation: Some countries, for example, Spain and Mexico, have very rich dialects.
examples.note: 'Por ejemplo' is the standard way to introduce an example. You can also use 'como' or 'tal como' for when you list examples within a sentence.

examples.original: No puedo acompañarte; o sea, tengo mucho trabajo.
examples.phonetic: /no ˈpwe.ðo a.kom.paˈɲaɾ.te o se.a ˈten.ɡo ˈmu.tʃo tɾaˈβa.xo/
examples.translation: I can't go with you; I mean, I have a lot of work.
examples.note: 'O sea' is very common in spoken Spanish to reformulate or explain, but avoid it in formal writing; use 'es decir' instead.

title: Matización y distanciamiento (Hedging and Tentativeness)
bridge: In English, hedging often relies on modal verbs (might, could, would) and adverbs (perhaps, possibly). Spanish has similar resources, but the structures differ: the Spanish subjunctive mood (especially the imperfect subjunctive with -ra) is crucial for expressing tentativeness, and verbs like 'parecer', 'resultar', and 'costar' carry nuance that doesn't map directly to English. A common trap is overusing the conditional in Spanish where English would use 'would'—Spanish often prefers the imperfect subjunctive. Also, Spanish can express hedging through impersonal 'se' constructions, which English lacks.
rule: To express hedging and tentativeness in Spanish at a C1 level, use: 1) The imperfect subjunctive (-ra form) after expressions of doubt, desire, or in conditional sentences (e.g., 'quisiera', 'pudiera', 'fuera'), often replacing the conditional in polite requests or hypotheticals. 2) Verbs like 'parecer' (to seem) with the subjunctive in subordinate clauses when negated or in questions (e.g., 'No parece que vaya a llover'). 3) The conditional simple (e.g., 'podría', 'sería') for hypothetical statements and polite suggestions, but note that in many contexts, especially after 'si' clauses, Spanish uses the imperfect subjunctive + conditional. 4) Adverbial hedges like 'quizás', 'tal vez', 'a lo mejor'—'quizás' and 'tal vez' can be followed by indicative or subjunctive (subjunctive when the doubt is stronger), while 'a lo mejor' always takes indicative. 5) Impersonal 'se' constructions: 'se podría decir que', 'se diría que' to distance the speaker. 6) The future tense can also be used to express conjecture (e.g., 'será verdad' = 'it may/might be true'). Avoid direct translation of English 'would' with conditional in all cases, as Spanish sometimes uses the imperfect indicative in polite expressions (e.g., 'quería saber si...').

concept_examples.text: Quizás tenga razón, pero no estoy seguro.
concept_examples.translation: Perhaps he/she is right, but I'm not sure.
concept_examples.phonetic: kiˈθas ˈteŋɡa raˈθon ˈpeɾo no esˈtoj seˈɣuɾo

concept_examples.text: Sería interesante considerar otras opciones.
concept_examples.translation: It would be interesting to consider other options.
concept_examples.phonetic: seˈɾia inteɾeˈsante konsideˈɾaɾ ˈotɾas opˈθjones

concept_examples.text: No parece que vaya a llover hoy.
concept_examples.translation: It doesn't seem like it's going to rain today.
concept_examples.phonetic: no paˈɾeθe ke ˈbaʝa a ʎoˈβeɾ oi

concept_examples.text: Se podría decir que la situación es compleja.
concept_examples.translation: One could say that the situation is complex.
concept_examples.phonetic: se poˈðɾia deˈθiɾ ke la situaˈθjon es komˈplexa

common_error.wrong: Si yo tendría tiempo, te ayudaría.
common_error.correct: Si yo tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría.
common_error.correct_alt: Si yo tuviese tiempo, te ayudaría.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use the conditional 'would' in both clauses of a conditional sentence, mirroring English ('If I would have time'). However, in Spanish, the 'si' (if) clause must always use the imperfect subjunctive (or pluperfect subjunctive) when referring to hypothetical or contrary-to-fact situations. The conditional is reserved for the result clause. Using 'tendría' after 'si' is grammatically incorrect. To avoid this error, remember: 'si + imperfect subjunctive' + 'conditional' (e.g., 'si tuviera tiempo, ayudaría').

examples.original: Quizás lleguemos tarde.
examples.phonetic: kiˈθas ʎeˈɣemos ˈtaɾðe
examples.translation: Perhaps we will arrive late.
examples.note: Note the use of the present subjunctive (lleguemos) after 'quizás' to express uncertainty. If the speaker were more certain, they might use the indicative 'llegamos'.

examples.original: Tal vez haya un problema con el sistema.
examples.phonetic: tal ˈbeθ ˈaʝa un pɾoˈβlema kon el sisˈtema
examples.translation: Maybe there is a problem with the system.
examples.note: 'Haya' is the present subjunctive of 'haber'. 'Tal vez' is similar to 'quizás' but slightly more formal.

examples.original: A lo mejor no viene hoy.
examples.phonetic: a lo meˈxoɾ no ˈbjene oi
examples.translation: Maybe he/she is not coming today.
examples.note: 'A lo mejor' always takes the indicative mood, unlike 'quizás' and 'tal vez' which can take subjunctive. This is a common pitfall for English speakers.

examples.original: Si tuviera más dinero, viajaría más.
examples.phonetic: si tuˈβjeɾa ˈmas diˈneɾo, bjaˈxaˈɾia mas
examples.translation: If I had more money, I would travel more.
examples.note: Imperfect subjunctive (tuviera) in the 'si' clause, conditional (viajaría) in the result clause. This is the standard structure for hypothetical situations.

examples.original: Pudiera ser que se haya equivocado.
examples.phonetic: puˈðjeɾa seɾ ke se ˈaʝa ekiβoˈkaðo
examples.translation: It could be that he/she has made a mistake.
examples.note: Here, the imperfect subjunctive 'pudiera' expresses a tentative possibility, more polite than 'puede ser'. The combination with 'haya' (perfect subjunctive) adds nuance.

examples.original: Quisiera pedirte un favor.
examples.phonetic: kiˈsjeɾa peˈðiɾte un faˈβoɾ
examples.translation: I would like to ask you a favor.
examples.note: This is a classic example of 'quisiera' used as a polite request instead of 'querría' or 'quiero'. It's a form of hedging that softens the request.

examples.original: Se diría que el gobierno no toma medidas.
examples.phonetic: se diˈɾia ke el ɣoˈβjeɾno no ˈtoma meˈðiðas
examples.translation: One would say that the government is not taking measures.
examples.note: The impersonal 'se' plus conditional 'diría' distances the speaker from the assertion, making it sound more objective and tentative.

examples.original: No es que no me guste, sino que tengo otras prioridades.
examples.phonetic: no es ke no me ˈɣuste, ˈsino ke ˈteŋɡo ˈotɾas pɾjoɾiˈðaðes
examples.translation: It's not that I don't like it, but rather that I have other priorities.
examples.note: The expression 'no es que + subjunctive' is a subtle way of hedging a negative opinion. The subjunctive 'guste' is required because of the negation and doubt.

examples.original: Me parece que podrías reconsiderar tu postura.
examples.phonetic: me paˈɾeθe ke poˈðɾias rekonsiðeˈɾaɾ tu posˈtuɾa
examples.translation: It seems to me that you could reconsider your stance.
examples.note: Using 'me parece que' with the conditional 'podrías' softens a suggestion, making it a polite recommendation rather than a direct command.

title: Patrones verbales complejos (objeto directo e indirecto) / Complex Verb Patterns (Double Object, etc.)
bridge: In English, we often rely on word order and prepositions to signal who receives what (e.g., 'I gave the book to him' vs. 'I gave him the book'). Spanish, however, uses a combination of prepositions (a), clitic pronouns (me, te, le, lo, la, etc.), and full noun phrases in a way that can confuse English speakers. A key trap is the use of 'le' and 'les' for indirect objects, which can be mistaken for direct object pronouns, especially in contexts with animate objects. Additionally, Spanish often duplicates the indirect object (both the pronoun and the full noun phrase) for clarity or emphasis, a structure that has no direct English equivalent. Understanding these patterns is essential for achieving C1 fluency and avoiding ambiguity.
rule: In Spanish, verbs can take both a direct object (DO) and an indirect object (IO). The IO is introduced by the preposition 'a' (personal 'a' for people or pets) and is often replaced or reinforced by the clitic pronouns 'le' (singular) and 'les' (plural). When both DO and IO are pronouns, the IO pronoun changes to 'se' to avoid the awkward 'le lo' combination. For example, 'Se lo di' (I gave it to him/her/them). The placement of object pronouns is flexible: they typically precede the conjugated verb (e.g., 'Te lo dije') or attach to infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative commands (e.g., 'decírtelo', 'diciéndomelo', 'dámelo'). At C1, you must also handle verbs that take both objects in complex tenses (e.g., with participles: 'Se lo he dado') and with subordinate clauses. The duplication of the IO with a full noun phrase (e.g., 'Le dije a María') is common in spoken Spanish, even when the pronoun alone suffices. Avoid the common error of using 'lo' for the IO when it refers to a person (e.g., 'Le vi' is correct for 'I saw him', not 'Lo vi' in some regions, but 'leísmo' is a dialectal variation). Mastery requires distinguishing between direct and indirect objects based on verb semantics and prepositions.

concept_examples.text: Se lo di ayer.
concept_examples.translation: I gave it to him/her/you (formal) yesterday.
concept_examples.phonetic: [se lo ˈdi aˈʝeɾ]

concept_examples.text: Le compré un regalo a mi madre.
concept_examples.translation: I bought a gift for my mother.
concept_examples.phonetic: [le komˈpɾe un reˈɣalo a mi ˈmaðɾe]

concept_examples.text: ¿Me lo puedes explicar?
concept_examples.translation: Can you explain it to me?
concept_examples.phonetic: [ˈme lo ˈpweðes ekspliˈkaɾ]

concept_examples.text: Dáselo a ellos, no a mí.
concept_examples.translation: Give it to them, not to me.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ˈdase lo a ˈeʝos no a mi]

common_error.wrong: Le dije a él que lo hiciera, pero luego lo dije a ella.
common_error.correct: Le dije a él que lo hiciera, pero luego se lo dije a ella.
common_error.correct_alt: Le dije a él que lo hiciera, pero luego se lo dije a ella.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because English speakers may directly translate 'I told him... and then I told it to her' without adjusting the pronoun combination. In Spanish, when the direct object is also a pronoun (e.g., 'lo'), the indirect object pronoun 'le' must change to 'se' to avoid the forbidden sequence 'le lo'. So 'se lo dije' means 'I told it to her/him/them'. The wrong form 'lo dije a ella' would mean 'I said it to her' only if the indirect object is not otherwise expressed, but with both objects, the correct pattern is 'se lo dije a ella'.

levels.label: Objeto indirecto y directo con verbos comunes
levels.translation: Indirect and direct object with common verbs

examples.original: Te doy el libro.
examples.phonetic: [te ˈdoi el ˈliβɾo]
examples.translation: I give you the book.
examples.note: Note that 'te' is the indirect object pronoun (to you) and 'el libro' is the direct object (thing). In English, we use word order to show this.

examples.original: Les explico la lección a los estudiantes.
examples.phonetic: [les eksˈpliko la lekˈθjon a los estuˈðjantes]
examples.translation: I explain the lesson to the students.
examples.note: The IO pronoun 'les' is duplicated by the full noun phrase 'a los estudiantes' for emphasis and clarity, which is common in Spanish.

levels.label: Combinación de pronombres de objeto (se lo, se la, etc.)
levels.translation: Combination of object pronouns (se lo, se la, etc.)

examples.original: Se lo dije ayer.
examples.phonetic: [se lo ˈdixe aˈʝeɾ]
examples.translation: I told it to him/her/you (formal) yesterday.
examples.note: When both IO and DO are third-person pronouns, 'le' or 'les' becomes 'se' to avoid the illegible 'le lo' or 'les lo'.

examples.original: ¿Se la enviaste a María?
examples.phonetic: [ˈse la emˈbjas te a maˈɾi.a]
examples.translation: Did you send it (feminine) to María?
examples.note: Here 'se' stands for 'a María' (to her) and 'la' is the direct object (e.g., the letter). The combination 'se la' is used.

examples.original: No se me ocurre cómo decírselo.
examples.phonetic: [no se me oˈkure ˈkomo deˈθiɾselo]
examples.translation: I can't think of how to tell it to him/her.
examples.note: The infinitive 'decírselo' attaches the pronouns to the end, with 'se' for the IO and 'lo' for the DO.

levels.label: Duplicación del objeto indirecto y posiciones en oraciones complejas
levels.translation: Indirect object duplication and positions in complex sentences

examples.original: A mis padres les encanta viajar, pero a mí no me gusta.
examples.phonetic: [a mis paˈðɾes les enˈkanta bjaˈxaɾ peɾo a mi no me ˈɣusta]
examples.translation: My parents love traveling, but I don't like it.
examples.note: In Spanish, the IO is often duplicated both before the verb (clitic) and after with a full noun phrase (a mis padres) for emphasis or clarity, a pattern that does not occur in English.

examples.original: Se lo he comprado yo, pero se lo di ayer.
examples.phonetic: [se lo e komˈpɾaðo ʝo peɾo se lo di aˈʝeɾ]
examples.translation: I have bought it for him/her, but I gave it to him/her yesterday.
examples.note: In compound tenses, the clitic pronouns precede the auxiliary verb 'he', not the participle.

examples.original: Si me lo hubieras dicho antes, te lo habría agradecido.
examples.phonetic: [si me lo uˈbjeɾas ˈditʃo ˈantes te lo aˈβɾia aɣɾaðeˈsiðo]
examples.translation: If you had told me before, I would have thanked you for it.
examples.note: In conditional and past subjunctive contexts, the pronoun order and combination remain fixed: 'me lo' and 'te lo'.

title: Matices entre tiempos y aspectos verbales / Nuances of Tense and Aspect
bridge: English speakers often rely on a binary between simple and progressive aspects, but Spanish adds layers of meaning through the contrast between preterite, imperfect, and perfect tenses, as well as the subtle use of the progressive with estar vs. the simple present. For example, while English says 'I was reading' for both a background action and an interrupted action, Spanish distinguishes between 'leía' (imperfect, habitual or ongoing past) and 'estaba leyendo' (progressive, emphasizing the action in progress). Also, the present perfect in Spanish ('he leído') connects a past action to the present moment, but in some contexts it can express a recent action that English would use the simple past for. The key trap is choosing the wrong aspect to express duration, iteration, or a changing state, especially in narration.
rule: At C1, you need to master the nuanced use of tense and aspect in Spanish. The preterite (e.g., 'leí') presents an action as a completed event with a defined beginning and end, while the imperfect (e.g., 'leía') describes ongoing, habitual, or background actions without focusing on completion. The perfect tenses (e.g., 'he leído') link a past action to the present or indicate relevance to now. The progressive (estar + gerund) emphasizes the ongoing nature of an action at a specific moment, but it is not used as often as in English; the simple present or imperfect often suffices for ongoing states. Also, the contrast between 'ser' and 'estar' can interact with aspect: 'ser' is used for inherent characteristics (e.g., 'es alto') while 'estar' for temporary states (e.g., 'está cansado'). For narration, the preterite advances the plot, while the imperfect sets the scene. Additionally, the conditional perfect ('habría hablado') and pluperfect ('había hablado') express hypothetical or prior actions relative to another time. Pay attention to verbs that change meaning with tense, such as 'conocer' (preterite: 'met' vs. imperfect: 'knew') and 'tener' (preterite: 'received' vs. imperfect: 'had').

concept_examples.text: Cuando llegué, ella ya había salido.
concept_examples.translation: When I arrived, she had already left.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈkwando ʝeˈɣe, ˈeʝa ʝa ˈaβja saˈliðo

concept_examples.text: Mientras leía, sonó el teléfono.
concept_examples.translation: While I was reading, the phone rang.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈmjentɾas leˈi.a, soˈno el teˈlefono

concept_examples.text: He vivido en Madrid durante diez años.
concept_examples.translation: I have lived in Madrid for ten years.
concept_examples.phonetic: e βiˈβiðo en maˈðɾið duˈɾante djeθ ˈaɲos

concept_examples.text: Estaba estudiando cuando me llamaste.
concept_examples.translation: I was studying when you called me.
concept_examples.phonetic: esˈtaβa estuˈðjando ˈkwando me ʝaˈmaste

common_error.wrong: Cuando era joven, comí mucho pan.
common_error.correct: Cuando era joven, comía mucho pan.
common_error.correct_alt: De joven, solía comer mucho pan.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often use the preterite for habitual past actions because the English simple past ('I ate') can express habit. In Spanish, however, habitual actions in the past require the imperfect. Using the preterite 'comí' implies a one-time completed event. To avoid this, think of the imperfect as the 'was -ing' or 'used to' aspect for describing past routines.

examples.original: Ayer estuve en casa todo el día.
examples.phonetic: aˈʝer esˈtuβe en ˈkasa ˈtoðo el ˈdi.a
examples.translation: Yesterday I was at home all day.
examples.note: Preterite 'estuve' emphasizes the complete duration within a defined time frame.

examples.original: Cuando era niño, vivía en el campo.
examples.phonetic: ˈkwando ˈeɾa ˈniɲo, biˈβi.a en el ˈkampo
examples.translation: When I was a child, I used to live in the countryside.
examples.note: Imperfect 'vivía' describes a past state without a defined end.

examples.original: De repente, oyó un ruido extraño.
examples.phonetic: de reˈpente, oˈʝo un ˈrwiðo eksˈtɾaɲo
examples.translation: Suddenly, he heard a strange noise.
examples.note: Preterite 'oyó' marks a specific event that interrupted an ongoing situation.

examples.original: Estoy leyendo un libro interesante.
examples.phonetic: esˈtoi leˈʝendo un ˈliβɾo inteɾeˈsante
examples.translation: I am reading an interesting book.
examples.note: Progressive emphasizes the action in progress right now.

examples.original: Vivo en Barcelona desde 2015.
examples.phonetic: ˈbiβo en baɾseˈlona ˈdezðe 2015
examples.translation: I have been living in Barcelona since 2015.
examples.note: Simple present 'vivo' expresses a state that began in the past and continues, whereas English uses present perfect progressive.

examples.original: Cuando me viste, estaba cocinando.
examples.phonetic: ˈkwando me ˈβiste, esˈtaβa kosiˈnando
examples.translation: When you saw me, I was cooking.
examples.note: Imperfect progressive 'estaba cocinando' sets the background action; the preterite 'viste' is the event.

levels.label: Perfecto y pluscuamperfecto para conectar momentos
levels.translation: Perfect and pluperfect for connecting moments

examples.original: Ya había comido cuando llegaste.
examples.phonetic: ʝa aˈβia koˈmiðo ˈkwando ʝeˈɣaste
examples.translation: I had already eaten when you arrived.
examples.note: Pluperfect 'había comido' expresses an action completed before another past action.

examples.original: Nunca he visitado Japón.
examples.phonetic: ˈnuŋka e βisiˈtaðo xaˈpon
examples.translation: I have never visited Japan.
examples.note: Present perfect 'he visitado' connects past experience to the present moment.

examples.original: Te llamé porque había pensado en ti.
examples.phonetic: te ʝaˈme ˈpoɾke ˈaβia penˈsaðo en ti
examples.translation: I called you because I had thought of you.
examples.note: Pluperfect 'había pensado' explains a prior reason for the preterite action.

title: Pasivas avanzadas (se cree que, se dice que, hay quien dice que) / Advanced passives (it is believed, there is said to be)
bridge: In English, advanced passives often use 'it' as a dummy subject: 'It is said that...' or 'There is said to be...'. Spanish achieves the same effect with impersonal 'se' plus a verb in the third person singular, or with 'se' plus an infinitive in more complex structures. The key trap is that Spanish does not use a dummy 'it' – the subject is always implicit in the verb ending or the pronoun 'se'. Also, Spanish prefers the passive 'se' over the 'ser' + participle passive in these impersonal constructions, whereas English often uses 'be + past participle'.
rule:
In Spanish, advanced passives (pasivas impersonales) express general belief, saying, or reporting without specifying an agent. The most common constructions are:

1. **'Se' + third person singular verb**: 'Se cree que...' (It is believed that...), 'Se dice que...' (It is said that...), 'Se piensa que...' (It is thought that...). This is the direct equivalent of the English 'it + passive'.
2. **'Se' + verb + infinitive**: For structures like 'There is said to be...', Spanish uses 'Se dice que hay...' or 'Se dice que existe...' rather than a passive infinitive. For example, 'Se dice que hay un tesoro' (There is said to be a treasure).
3. **'Hay' + noun + 'que' + verb**: 'Hay quien dice que...' (There are those who say that...) – an alternative construction that is less impersonal but common.
4. **Passive 'se' with 'decir', 'creer', 'pensar', 'saber', 'considerar', 'afirmar', etc.** – these verbs can also appear in the passive 'se' form with a following clause or infinitive: 'Se sabe que...' (It is known that...), 'Se considera que...' (It is considered that...).
5. **Impersonal 'se' with indirect object**: When the verb is transitive and there is an indirect object, Spanish can use 'se' + verb + indirect object + que-clause: 'Se me dijo que...' (I was told that...), 'Se le cree inteligente' (He is believed intelligent).
6. **Avoid overusing 'ser' passives**: While 'Es creído que' might be understood, it is unnatural. Spanish prefers the 'se' construction.
7. **Tense and mood**: The verb in the 'se' construction can be in any tense – present, preterite, imperfect, future, conditional, and subjunctive – depending on the sentence. For example, 'Se creía que era imposible' (It was believed that it was impossible).
8. **Use with infinitives**: With perception verbs, Spanish can use 'se' + verb + infinitive: 'Se le ve llegar' (He is seen arriving/to arrive), but this is less common.

Typical use cases: news reports, academic writing, formal registers, expressing general opinion or beliefs.

concept_examples.text: Se cree que el cambio climático es irreversible.
concept_examples.translation: It is believed that climate change is irreversible.
concept_examples.phonetic: se ˈkɾe.e ke el ˈtʃam.bjo kliˈma.ti.ko es i.re.βerˈsi.βle/

concept_examples.text: Se dice que hay un tesoro escondido en esta isla.
concept_examples.translation: There is said to be a hidden treasure on this island.
concept_examples.phonetic: se ˈdi.se ke ˈai̯ un teˈso.ɾo es.konˈdi.ðo en ˈes.ta ˈis.la/

concept_examples.text: Se sabe que los números primos son infinitos.
concept_examples.translation: It is known that prime numbers are infinite.
concept_examples.phonetic: se ˈsa.βe ke los ˈnu.me.ɾos ˈpɾi.mos son in.fiˈni.tos/

concept_examples.text: Se me dijo que la reunión se había cancelado.
concept_examples.translation: I was told that the meeting had been cancelled.
concept_examples.phonetic: se me ˈdi.xo ke la reuˈnjon se aˈβi.a kan.θeˈla.ðo/

common_error.wrong: Es creído que el problema es complejo.
common_error.correct: Se cree que el problema es complejo.
common_error.correct_alt: Se considera que el problema es complejo.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often try to translate 'it is believed' with a literal 'es + past participle' structure ('es creído'). However, in Spanish, this 'ser' passive with an impersonal meaning is ungrammatical or very unnatural. Spanish uses the reflexive passive 'se' with a third-person verb. The only exception is with certain verbs like 'decir' but even then 'se dice' is much more common than 'es dicho'. To avoid this error, remember that for impersonal passives, use 'se' + verb in the third person singular.

levels.label: Se impersonal con verbos de opinión

examples.original: Se cree que el nuevo presidente cambiará la política.
examples.phonetic: se ˈkɾe.e ke el ˈnwe.βo pɾe.siˈðen.te kam.bjaˈɾa la poˈli.ti.ka/
examples.translation: It is believed that the new president will change politics.
examples.note: Use 'se cree' for 'it is believed'. Notice the verb agrees with the singular subject that follows.

examples.original: Se piensa que la economía mejorará el próximo año.
examples.phonetic: se ˈpjen.sa ke la e.ko.noˈmi.a me.xo.ɾaˈɾa el ˈpɾok.si.mo ˈa.ɲo/
examples.translation: It is thought that the economy will improve next year.
examples.note: 'Se piensa' is equivalent to 'it is thought'. The subordinate clause is in the future tense.

examples.original: Se considera que el proyecto es viable.
examples.phonetic: se kon.siˈde.ɾa ke el pɾoˈʝek.to es ˈβja.βle/
examples.translation: It is considered that the project is viable.
examples.note: 'Se considera' works like 'it is considered'. This is common in academic contexts.

levels.label: Se dice y otras construcciones de reporte

examples.original: Se dice que el ministro va a dimitir.
examples.phonetic: se ˈdi.se ke el miˈnis.tɾo βa a di.miˈtiɾ/
examples.translation: It is said that the minister is going to resign.
examples.note: This is the exact equivalent of 'it is said that'. Note that 'se dice' is much more frequent than 'es dicho'.

examples.original: Se rumorea que van a cerrar la fábrica.
examples.phonetic: se ru.moˈɾe.a ke βan a θeˈraɾ la ˈfa.βɾi.ka/
examples.translation: It is rumored that they are going to close the factory.
examples.note: 'Se rumorea' is a less formal but common way to report rumors.

examples.original: Se afirma que los resultados son fiables.
examples.phonetic: se aˈfiɾ.ma ke los re.sulˈta.ðos son ˈfja.βles/
examples.translation: It is affirmed that the results are reliable.
examples.note: 'Se afirma' is used in formal or academic contexts to state something confidently.

examples.original: Se me informó de que había un retraso.
examples.phonetic: se me in.foɾˈmo de ke aˈβi.a un reˈtɾa.so/
examples.translation: I was informed that there was a delay.
examples.note: Here 'me' is the indirect object. The structure is 'se' + verb + indirect object pronoun. It's equivalent to 'I was informed' in English.

examples.original: Se le aconsejó que no invirtiera en esa empresa.
examples.phonetic: se le a.kon.seˈxo ke no im.biɾˈtje.ɾa en ˈe.sa emˈpɾe.sa/
examples.translation: He/She was advised not to invest in that company.
examples.note: 'Se le aconsejó' uses 'le' as the indirect object. The verb is in the preterite, and the subordinate clause uses the subjunctive because it is an indirect command.

examples.original: Se nos recuerda que mañana es el plazo final.
examples.phonetic: se nos reˈkweɾ.ða ke maˈɲa.na es el ˈpla.θo fiˈnal/
examples.translation: We are reminded that tomorrow is the final deadline.
examples.note: Here 'nos' (us) is the indirect object. The structure is common in reminders and announcements.

translations.en: Advanced passives (it is believed, there is said to be)
